entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Mughal Empire (1526–1857) was an Islamic empire that at its height controlled most of the Indian subcontinent, ruling over 150 million people — a quarter of the world's population. Founded by Babur, a prince from Fergana Valley (Uzbekistan) descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, the Mughals created an extraordinary synthesis of Persian, Turkic, and Indian cultures.

Akbar the Great (r.1556-1605) expanded the empire to its greatest extent while implementing a policy of religious tolerance (Sulh-e-Kul, 'universal peace'), abolishing the jizya tax on Hindus, marrying Hindu Rajput princess Jodha Bai, and creating a composite Mughal-Rajput cultural synthesis. Akbar's court produced extraordinary painting, literature, and architecture, while his revenue system designed by finance minister Raja Todar Mal set the fiscal foundation for both Mughal prosperity and later British administration.

Shah Jahan (r.1628-1658) built the Taj Mahal as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal — one of history's supreme architectural achievements. At its peak, the Mughal Empire generated 25% of world GDP. Its decline under Aurangzeb's religious intolerance and subsequent fragmentation enabled British East India Company expansion that culminated in the 1857 Rebellion and formal dissolution of the dynasty.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Mughal Empire unified South Asia under sophisticated administration, created enduring monuments, and generated 25% of world GDP at its peak, leaving cultural legacies that define India's art, cuisine, language, and architecture today.
